title: Distributed Consistency and Failure Lab
description: Reason about replicas, consistency, consensus, distributed commit, partitions, idempotent retries, and conflict policies using a last-seat booking lab.

references.title: Database System Concepts: distributed database slides

questions.question_text: What does replication do?
questions.explanation: Copies and their guarantees must be analyzed separately.

questions.question_text: What does partitioning do?
questions.explanation: Partitioning distributes portions of the dataset.

questions.question_text: A acknowledged write is absent from an asynchronous follower read. What is a likely explanation?
questions.explanation: The follower may not yet have received the acknowledged write.

questions.question_text: Which property explicitly respects real time order of completed operations?
questions.explanation: Linearizability places effects between invocation and response and respects real time.

questions.question_text: Does serializability alone imply linearizability?
questions.explanation: Serial equivalence and real time ordering are different requirements.

questions.question_text: What does eventual consistency alone fail to specify?
options: An exact freshness deadline for each read
questions.explanation: Eventual convergence does not supply a per-read freshness deadline.

questions.question_text: What is read your writes?
options: Every writer gets an exclusive server
A session can observe its own completed writes under the contract
Every query must use SELECT FOR UPDATE
questions.explanation: This is a session guarantee rather than universal freshness.

questions.question_text: What is a core role of consensus?
options: Agreement on a decision or ordered history
questions.explanation: Consensus coordinates agreement under a defined failure model.

questions.question_text: What failure class does the basic Raft model target?
options: Arbitrary malicious behavior by every node
questions.explanation: The standard model does not cover arbitrary Byzantine participants.

questions.question_text: What question does distributed atomic commit answer?
options: Whether all transaction participants commit or abort
questions.explanation: Atomic commit coordinates one outcome across participants.

questions.question_text: Why can a prepared participant block in classic two phase commit?
options: It is allowed to invent a commit
It must learn the coordinator’s decision
The client must always be online
questions.explanation: A prepared participant cannot safely choose an independent contrary outcome.

questions.question_text: Does a client timeout prove a distributed transaction aborted?
options: Only when the request has an identifier
questions.explanation: The decision may have been committed while the response was lost.

questions.question_text: What is a network partition?
questions.explanation: Nodes may remain alive while unable to exchange messages.

questions.question_text: What is unsafe when promising a single final seat owner during partition?
options: Both sides independently confirming the seat
Serving a stale event description with its contract
questions.explanation: Conflicting confirmations violate the single-owner promise.

questions.question_text: Which retry identity supports deduplication?
options: A new identifier for each transmission
The same stable identifier for the same intention
questions.explanation: A stable operation identity lets the server recognize a repeated intention.

questions.question_text: Where should the operation identifier be recorded?
options: Atomically with its trusted business effect and outcome
questions.explanation: Recording identity and effect together closes a duplication window.

questions.question_text: How handle an identifier reused with different input?
options: Reject or resolve it under an explicit mismatch contract
questions.explanation: Identity reuse must not permit conflicting intentions to masquerade as a retry.

questions.question_text: Does idempotent processing imply exactly once network delivery?
questions.explanation: Repeated delivery can be handled without repeated business effects.

questions.question_text: Why can last writer wins be wrong for seat allocation?
options: Discarding a conflict can break already promised ownership
It removes the need for coordination
questions.explanation: Merge policies must respect the business invariant.

questions.question_text: Which experiment provides distributed failure evidence?
options: One ordinary SELECT on one node
Controlled delayed-message and retry tests with outcome checks
questions.explanation: Fault and recovery behavior requires exercising the relevant distributed paths.

notes:
## Start with one business operation

A distributed database stores or processes data across multiple networked machines. Replication places copies of data on different nodes; partitioning divides data so different nodes own different portions. A system can use both. The motivation might be fault tolerance, proximity to users, storage capacity, or workload distribution. None of these mechanisms automatically proves that a particular business operation is correct. Start by defining the operation and the failures it must tolerate.

Consider a campus event with one remaining seat. A booking request should either reserve that seat once or return an appropriate rejection. It must not create two confirmed reservations, even if a response is lost and the client retries. This tiny example exposes replication freshness, coordination, idempotency, and failure handling without requiring a production cluster. We will reason about explicit histories rather than claiming that a single local query demonstrates distributed safety.

## Distinguish copies from guarantees

Suppose node A accepts writes and node B follows asynchronously. A records reservation R and acknowledges it before B receives the change. A subsequent read from B may still show the seat available. This is replication lag. Replication improves the number of places data can survive, but asynchronous copying alone does not guarantee that every read reflects the latest acknowledged write. A failover to a lagging copy also needs an explicit policy for potentially missing writes.

Strong consistency is an overloaded phrase, so name the intended property. Linearizability presents each completed operation as taking effect at one point between its invocation and response, respecting real time order. Serializability concerns transaction equivalence to a serial execution and does not by itself impose that real time rule. Eventual consistency describes convergence under appropriate conditions after updates cease; it does not state how soon a particular read becomes fresh or what every intermediate read may return.

Session guarantees can be narrower and useful. Read your writes means a session can observe its own completed writes through the documented routing and consistency mechanism. Monotonic reads prevent that session from moving backward to older observed states. Neither should be assumed merely because a client reuses the same user identifier. Ask how the database or application carries the necessary session context when requests are routed between replicas.

## Separate consensus from distributed commit

Consensus coordinates agreement on a decision or ordered history among participants under a specified failure model. Raft is a well known protocol for a replicated state machine with leader election and log replication, designed for non Byzantine failures. A majority can make progress under its stated assumptions while a minority cannot independently accept conflicting authoritative history. This is a protocol guarantee, not permission to ignore stable storage, membership changes, or the implementation's documented limits.

Distributed commit asks whether several transaction participants should all commit or all abort one transaction. Classic two phase commit first asks participants to prepare, then records and communicates a commit or abort decision. A participant that has prepared cannot simply invent its own outcome when the coordinator is unavailable. Prepared work can therefore block pending recovery of the decision. Replicating the coordinator with consensus can improve aspects of the design, but consensus and atomic commit remain different problems with different roles.

```text
Booking transaction spans Seat shard and Payment ledger shard.
1. Coordinator asks both participants to prepare.
2. Seat says ready; ledger says ready.
3. Coordinator durably decides commit.
4. Coordinator notifies both participants.
```

If the coordinator fails after step three but before one notification, the durable decision still matters. The uninformed participant must recover the decision through the protocol rather than casually aborting a prepared change. If failure occurs before a decision, recovery follows the documented protocol state. Do not reason solely from which client saw a timeout: a timeout says the caller lacks an answer, not that every participant performed an abort.

## Reason about a network partition

A network partition prevents some nodes from communicating even when the machines themselves remain alive. During a partition, a system requiring one authoritative seat allocation must coordinate which side can approve a booking. Allowing both sides to approve the same last seat without coordination creates a conflict that later merging cannot erase as if neither student received a promise. The availability and consistency decision concerns concrete operations under the partition, rather than a permanent label attached to the entire product.

A useful design can keep some operations available while rejecting others. A cached event description may be safely served with a freshness label, while confirmation of the final seat requires the authoritative path. This difference follows from the business contract. It is misleading to require every read and write to use the same trade off merely because they share a database. Document what a caller receives when the authoritative path is unavailable: a retryable failure, a pending request, or a deliberately weaker promise.

## Make retries safe through identity

Assign the intended booking a stable operation identifier before submitting it. The trusted database operation must atomically record that identifier and its outcome with the booking effect. If the reply is lost, the client retries using the same identifier or queries its recorded outcome. A uniqueness constraint helps prevent applying the same identified action twice. Generating a fresh identifier for each retry defeats that protection because the database sees distinct operations.

Idempotency is not a claim that messages are delivered exactly once. Networks and workers may deliver requests repeatedly, and response loss remains possible. The goal is that repeated processing of the same identified intention produces one business effect and a consistent response contract. Define how long identifiers remain recognized, what happens when the same identifier carries different input, and how concurrent duplicate attempts synchronize. Expiration and payload mismatch are correctness cases, not just cleanup details.

## Conflicts need a business policy

If two disconnected users edit a descriptive note, the system might preserve both versions and ask for a merge. Last writer wins is another possible policy, but clocks, causality, and lost edits need analysis. A larger timestamp does not prove a more correct human decision. For quantities such as seats or money, discarding a conflicting value may violate invariants. Choose conflict handling per data type and operation rather than making one universal merge rule.

Commutative operations can sometimes tolerate reordering, but duplicate delivery still matters. Adding one to a counter twice is not the same as adding it once. An operation based design needs stable identity or a suitable replicated data type protocol to distinguish repeated delivery from distinct increments. This is why claims about automatic convergence must state the supported operations and assumptions. A converged wrong reservation count is still wrong.

## Solved failure exercises

Exercise one: A acknowledges booking R, B still shows the seat open, and the next request reads B. Identify the issue. This is a stale replica read under the stated asynchronous design. Possible responses include routing the critical read to an authoritative path, using an appropriate consistency option, or making the interface tolerate and label stale information. The correct choice depends on whether the read merely displays information or authorizes another booking.

Exercise two: the client loses the reply after R commits and retries with identifier R again. What should the trusted operation return? It should discover the existing outcome and avoid a second booking effect. If the same identifier now names a different event, reject the mismatch according to the contract. Exercise three: both sides of a partition attempt to allocate the final seat. A design promising one confirmed owner must prevent independent conflicting approvals; accepting pending requests is different from confirming both.

To review a design, list nodes, authoritative records, acknowledgment points, replica routing, duplicate handling, and recovery states. Test delayed messages, repeated requests, leader failure, and reconciliation in an isolated environment before claiming operational evidence. Continue with [durability](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/durability) and [transaction boundaries](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/transaction-boundaries) to connect local commit guarantees with distributed outcomes.
